In DP Music the annotated bibliography is a **planning task**. It's where you show, before you write or play
anything, that your research rests on sources an examiner would accept. Each component's task asks for different
sources and different annotations; the course book's
[task references](https://dp-music.seancoleman.org/book/exploring-tasks.html) have the details. This lesson takes
each one in turn.

It assumes [Sources 3](sources-dp.qmd), on what examiners say about research and evidence, and
[Annotated Bibliography 2](annotate-check.qmd), on MLA format and evaluative annotations. Use MLA throughout.
Whatever the format, clear attribution and in-text citations are what matter most.

## Exploring Music in Context

**Your bibliography must include:**

- a **visual representation** of the piece you selected (a score, a lead sheet, a transcription or a graphic score)
- a **recording** of the piece
- **at least one journal article or book chapter**
- **one other high-quality source**

**Annotations:**

- For the **visual representation** and the **recording**: briefly explain the resource's strengths and why you
  chose it.
- For the **other two**: a summary of the source as it relates to your Exploring report, in two to four sentences each.

**Submit three files:** the annotated bibliography (PDF), the score or visual representation (PDF), and an audio
excerpt of the reference recording, cut to one minute (MP3).

**What makes these strong:**

- **The score:** say what edition it is, and why it's authoritative. Is it a published edition, the composer's own,
  or a scholarly transcription? A MuseScore upload is not an authentic score (see [Sources 3](sources-dp.qmd)). If
  it's all there is, say how you checked it against the recording.
- **The recording:** give full release details. Say why this performance: is it the original, a recording by the
  tradition's own performers, a historically informed one? Your one-minute excerpt is the start of your Upload 3, so
  choose it with your Section 1 timestamps in mind.
- **The article or chapter:** summarise only the part that bears on your report. Name the conventions or context it
  gives you that you can test against the music.

**Model annotation** for a recording (its form, not a template to copy):

> Davis, Miles. "So What." *Kind of Blue*, Columbia, 1959.
>
> The original studio recording, by the sextet that first played the piece. I chose it over later live versions
> because it is the session that Ashley Kahn's history of the album studies. Its slow-moving harmony (long stretches on one mode)
> is clear here, which gives me precise timestamps for Section 1.

## Experimenting with Music: as a performer

**Your bibliography must include, at a minimum:**

- a **recording** of someone performing the piece you selected
- a recording showing a **different interpretation**
- a recording of a **different piece** that includes a technique or interpretation you'll use to transform your stimulus
- **notation** for the piece you selected
- **written and/or video analysis or instruction** about the piece or a technique you've chosen to experiment with

**Annotations:** explain how you'll use each resource as you carry out Exercise 1. If you have ideas for Exercises 2
and 3, include them. Submit one PDF.

**What makes these strong:**

- The task is about **use**, so each annotation should name a decision: "I'll take the shorter phrasing in bars 1–8
  from this recording," not "this is a good recording."
- The two recordings of your piece should differ in a way you can name and point to (tempo, ornamentation,
  articulation, rubato). If you can't say how they differ, find a more different second recording.
- The "different piece" is where your transformation comes from. Say exactly which technique you're borrowing, and
  where in that recording it happens.
- This feeds Criterion C (rationale and commentary). An annotation that already explains *why* you'll make a choice
  is the start of a purposeful rationale.

**Model annotation** for written instruction:

> Chaffin, Roger, and Gabriela Imreh. "'Pulling Teeth and Torture': Musical Memory and Problem Solving." *Thinking
> and Reasoning*, vol. 3, no. 4, 1997, pp. 315–36.
>
> A case study of a concert pianist preparing a Bach piece. Her practice segments followed the piece's formal
> structure. I'll plan my first experiment the same way, practising and recording it phrase by phrase, and use the
> study in my commentary to explain why I divided the stimulus where I did.

## Collaborative Musical Project (HL)

This task has two parts.

**Part 1: Problem identification.** Name two or three problems that now stand between you and finishing your
project. Problems are things that need a solution. They show growth, not that something has gone wrong. For each,
write one or two sentences: what you already know, and why the problem matters to the project.

**Part 2: Annotated bibliography.** For each problem, find a high-quality source that will help you solve it. Write a
two-to-four-sentence annotation for each. Submit both parts as a single PDF.

**What makes these strong:**

- **A specific problem leads to a specific source.** "Rehearsals are disorganised" is hard to research. "Our
  drummer and bassist drift apart in the bridge, and I don't know how to rehearse a rhythm section" leads somewhere.
- **The source should come from someone who knows:** a rehearsal-technique text, a conductor's or producer's
  interview, a recording-engineering manual, an article on collaborative creativity.
- **Say what you'll try.** End the annotation with the step you'll take and how you'll know whether it worked. That
  is the beginning of the process evidence CMM rewards.

## From annotated bibliography to final submission

- **The annotated bibliography is not your final bibliography.** The submission needs a plain bibliography, with
  every score, recording and secondary source, plus in-text references at every point you use a source.
- **Annotations are a draft of your thinking, not a draft of your text.** Don't paste them into the report. Write
  fresh, and cite.
- **Keep it up to date.** When you add or drop a source, change the bibliography the same day.

## Paraphrasing

Each task carries the same advice, from Kate Turabian: read the passage, look away, think about it, and paraphrase it
while still looking away. Then run your finger along your sentence. If you find the same ideas in the same order in
the source, so will your reader. Try again.

## AI summaries are not sources

::: {.callout-important}
## No AI-generated summary belongs in a DP annotated bibliography as a source

- A Google AI Overview or a chatbot answer has no author, no stable text, and no way for an examiner to check it. It
  is not a primary source and it is not musicology. Listing it as a source shows only that the research stopped
  where it started.
- AI tools invent references: plausible authors, titles, journals and DOIs that don't exist. **Every entry in your
  bibliography must be a source you've found and read, watched or listened to yourself.**
- The IB doesn't regard work produced, even in part, by an AI tool as yours. If your school allows you to use AI at
  all, its output must be credited in the text and in the bibliography, like any quotation. Crediting it still
  doesn't make it evidence for a claim about the music.
- **What to do instead:** if an AI answer gave you a lead, trace it to a real source (a journal article, a book
  chapter, *Grove Music Online*, an interview, a score, a recording). Read it, and annotate that.
:::

## Check before you submit

- Every required source type is there, for this component's task.
- Each entry is complete MLA, in alphabetical order, under the heading **Annotated Bibliography**.
- Each annotation says what's needed: strengths and reasons, a summary as it pertains to your report, how you'll use
  it, or how it solves a named problem.
- Annotations are in your own words, with no quotation from the source.
- No AI summaries, and nothing you haven't read, heard or watched.
- For Exploring: the score PDF and the one-minute MP3 are attached.
